P0010.description: P0010 is a camshaft timing, actuator, or VVT fault. Start with oil quality and circuit checks, then prove whether the fault is solenoid, control, sensor, or mechanical timing.
possible_causes: Low oil level, dirty oil, wrong viscosity, sludge, or restricted oil passage
Camshaft actuator solenoid stuck, clogged screen, or poor oil control
Open, shorted, corroded, or oil-contaminated VVT solenoid connector or harness
Camshaft position sensor, crankshaft position sensor, or correlation problem
Stretched timing chain, worn guides, weak tensioner, slipped timing, or phaser issue
PCM control fault only after oil, circuit, command, and mechanical timing checks pass
quick_checks: Check oil level, oil condition, viscosity, service history, and sludge before replacing VVT parts
Inspect actuator solenoid connector, terminal tension, oil intrusion, screen debris, and harness routing
Command the VVT solenoid with a scan tool where supported and compare desired versus actual cam angle
Check solenoid resistance, power, ground, and control signal for circuit codes
If timing performance codes return, inspect cam/crank correlation, timing chain stretch, phaser movement, and oil pressure
Verify repair with hot idle, road test, commanded cam movement, and no pending timing codes

P0100.description: P0100 is a MAF circuit or airflow plausibility fault. Confirm intake sealing, airflow data, and circuit integrity before replacing the MAF sensor.
causes: Contaminated MAF sensing element, aftermarket oiled filter residue, or debris
Intake duct split, loose clamp, air-box leak, or unmetered air after the MAF
Restricted air filter, blocked intake path, or throttle-body airflow issue
MAF connector corrosion, loose terminal, open, short, or poor ground
Fuel delivery or exhaust leak problem making airflow data look implausible
diagnostic_steps: Inspect air filter, air box, intake tube, clamps, PCV hoses, and throttle-body ducting
Compare MAF grams per second to expected hot-idle and snap-throttle behavior
Review fuel trims with MAF data before replacing the sensor
Check connector terminal tension, power, ground, and signal where the code is circuit related
Smoke test for intake leaks if lean codes, rough idle, or high idle are present
Verify repair with stable trims, normal MAF data, and no hesitation on road test
possible_causes: Contaminated MAF sensing element, aftermarket oiled filter residue, or debris
Intake duct split, loose clamp, air-box leak, or unmetered air after the MAF

MAF connector corrosion, loose terminal, open, short, or poor ground

P0110.description: P0110 is an intake-air or engine-coolant temperature sensor/circuit fault. Separate false sensor data from a real temperature problem before replacing parts.
possible_causes: IAT or ECT sensor unplugged, biased, shorted, open, or contaminated
Connector corrosion, coolant intrusion, loose terminals, or damaged harness
Low coolant, trapped air, thermostat fault, cooling fan fault, or real overheating for ECT-related codes
Intake heat soak, damaged MAF/IAT assembly, or intake duct issue for IAT-related codes
Reference voltage, ground, or PCM input issue after sensor and wiring checks
quick_checks: Compare sensor readings to ambient temperature before start-up and to actual engine condition when warm
Inspect connector fit, terminal tension, corrosion, coolant intrusion, rub-through, and harness routing
Check reference voltage, ground, and signal response when the reading is stuck high or low
For ECT faults, verify coolant level, trapped air, thermostat operation, fan operation, and actual temperature
For IAT faults, inspect the intake path, MAF/IAT assembly, and heat-soak conditions
Verify repair with plausible cold-start readings, warm-up behavior, and no pending sensor codes

P0120.description: P0120 is a throttle position, pedal position, or correlation fault. Confirm sensor sweep, circuit integrity, and throttle movement before replacing the throttle body.
possible_causes: Throttle position sensor or pedal position sensor signal dropout or disagreement
Dirty, sticking, or carboned throttle plate
Throttle body connector corrosion, loose terminals, poor 5V reference, ground, or signal circuit
Damaged wiring near engine movement, prior repair disturbance, or water intrusion
Throttle body motor or internal sensor failure after circuit and mechanical checks
PCM or relearn issue only after voltage, ground, and command checks pass
quick_checks: Check for limp mode, reduced power message, and related APP/TPS correlation codes
Inspect throttle body bore, plate movement, connector, terminal tension, and harness routing
Graph TPS and APP signals while slowly sweeping the pedal and throttle command
Verify 5V reference, ground, and signal circuits before replacing the throttle body
Clean throttle deposits only when allowed by service information, then perform relearn if required
Confirm repair with stable idle, smooth pedal sweep data, and no reduced-power return

P0130.description: P0130 is an oxygen or air-fuel sensor circuit, signal, or heater fault for Bank 1 Sensor 1. The code points to a test path, not automatic sensor failure.

Melted, shorted, open, or corroded wiring near exhaust heat
Blown heater fuse, poor ground, or missing heater feed
Exhaust leak before the sensor altering oxygen content
Rich, lean, misfire, fuel pressure, or MAF problem making sensor data look wrong
Catalyst issue only after upstream fuel control and sensor operation are checked
diagnostic_steps: Confirm exact bank and sensor location before testing or replacing anything
Inspect exhaust-area wiring, connectors, clips, and melted insulation
For heater codes, check fuse, power, ground, and heater resistance before replacing the sensor
For signal codes, compare sensor activity, fuel trims, exhaust leaks, and fuel-control data
Do not replace downstream sensors for catalyst codes unless sensor behavior proves the sensor path
Verify repair with closed-loop operation, heater readiness, sensor response, and no pending codes

P0171.description: P0171 means Bank 1 fuel trim has gone lean. The code does not prove an oxygen sensor failed; use trim behavior to separate air leaks, MAF reporting, fuel delivery, and exhaust leaks.
causes: Vacuum leak, intake duct leak, PCV leak, brake-booster leak, or intake manifold gasket leak after the MAF
Dirty, contaminated, biased, or under-reporting MAF sensor
Low fuel pressure, restricted fuel filter, weak pump, or poor fuel volume under load
Exhaust leak ahead of the upstream oxygen or air-fuel sensor
Injector restriction, fuel contamination, or bank-specific air leak
Sensor feedback problem only after air leaks and fuel delivery are checked
diagnostic_steps: Review short- and long-term fuel trims at hot idle, 2500 RPM, cruise, and under load
If trims are most positive at idle, smoke test intake, PCV, brake-booster, and manifold gasket leak paths
If trims worsen under load, test fuel pressure, fuel volume, pump current, and restricted fuel delivery
Inspect intake boot clamps, air box sealing, MAF contamination, and aftermarket oiled filter residue
Check for exhaust leaks near the manifold or upstream sensor before replacing oxygen sensors
Confirm the repair by watching trims return near normal after clearing codes and road testing

Injector restriction, fuel contamination, or bank-specific air leak
Sensor feedback problem only after air leaks and fuel delivery are checked

MAF over-reporting airflow or intake sensor data biased warm or cold
Evap purge valve stuck open and pulling fuel vapor at idle
Oxygen or air-fuel sensor feedback problem after fuel and airflow checks
Engine coolant temperature data biased cold, causing added fuel
diagnostic_steps: Compare fuel trims, oxygen sensor activity, coolant temperature, MAF data, and purge command at hot idle
Check fuel pressure and injector leak-down before replacing sensors
Pinch or command purge closed where appropriate to see whether trims improve
Inspect air filter, intake tract, and MAF sensor condition
Verify repair with trims, tailpipe smell, idle quality, and readiness monitor behavior

Harness damage from heat, vibration, rodents, or previous engine work
quick_checks: Confirm the affected cylinder and compare with misfire counters and fuel-trim data
Inspect injector connector fit, terminals, harness routing, and shared power feed

Measure injector resistance and compare with matching injectors on the same engine
Check power feed, control-side voltage drop, shorts to power/ground, and continuity before replacing the injector
Verify repair with smooth idle, no misfire counters, and no pending injector circuit code

P0300.description: P0300 indicates the PCM detected a combustion misfire. Treat the code as a starting point for testing spark, fuel, air, and mechanical condition before replacing parts.
causes: Worn, fouled, cracked, or incorrectly gapped spark plug
Ignition coil or coil boot breaking down under heat or load
Injector restricted, leaking, unplugged, or not being commanded correctly
Vacuum leak, intake runner leak, PCV leak, or unmetered air affecting one or more cylinders
Low compression, valve sealing issue, timing issue, or head gasket seep
Fuel pressure or volume problem on random or multiple-cylinder misfires
diagnostic_steps: Record freeze-frame data and identify whether the misfire is cold-start, idle, cruise, or load related
Check live misfire counters and note whether the fault stays on one cylinder or moves between cylinders
Inspect plugs, coil boots, connectors, harness routing, oil intrusion, coolant evidence, and carbon tracking
Swap coil or plug only when the test can prove whether the misfire follows the part
Verify injector pulse, injector balance, and fuel pressure or volume when ignition checks pass
Perform compression, leak-down, relative compression, or cooling-system pressure checks before condemning mechanical parts
possible_causes: Worn, fouled, cracked, or incorrectly gapped spark plug
Ignition coil or coil boot breaking down under heat or load
Injector restricted, leaking, unplugged, or not being commanded correctly
Vacuum leak, intake runner leak, PCV leak, or unmetered air affecting one or more cylinders
Low compression, valve sealing issue, timing issue, or head gasket seep

Perform compression, leak-down, relative compression, or cooling-system pressure checks before condemning mechanical parts
symptoms: Rough idle, shaking, or engine vibration
Flashing or steady check engine light
Fuel smell, poor fuel economy, or catalyst overheating risk

P0420.description: P0420 indicates catalyst efficiency below threshold on Bank 1. Confirm converter efficiency only after checking sensor data, exhaust leaks, and upstream engine health.

Aftermarket converter efficiency below monitor threshold

After repair, complete the catalyst monitor drive cycle and confirm no pending efficiency codes return

P0440.description: P0440 is an EVAP leak, flow, or control fault. The code identifies a system problem, not a guaranteed purge valve, vent valve, canister, or gas cap failure.

Cracked EVAP hose, canister fitting, tank seal, rollover valve, or filler neck
Purge valve leaking when commanded closed
Vent valve stuck, restricted, contaminated, or not sealing
Fuel tank pressure sensor data or EVAP wiring fault
Charcoal canister damage or fuel saturation
diagnostic_steps: Confirm fuel level and freeze-frame conditions because EVAP monitors run only under specific conditions
Inspect fuel cap, filler neck, tank area, canister, hoses, and quick-connect fittings before replacing valves

Command purge and vent valves with a scan tool and verify both electrical response and physical sealing
Check vent filter restriction and refueling complaints when vent codes or pump click-off complaints exist
After repair, clear codes and run the EVAP monitor or service bay test when supported

P2135.description: P2135 is a throttle position, pedal position, or correlation fault. Confirm sensor sweep, circuit integrity, and throttle movement before replacing the throttle body.
possible_causes: Throttle position sensor or pedal position sensor signal dropout or disagreement
Dirty, sticking, or carboned throttle plate
Throttle body connector corrosion, loose terminals, poor 5V reference, ground, or signal circuit
Damaged wiring near engine movement, prior repair disturbance, or water intrusion
Throttle body motor or internal sensor failure after circuit and mechanical checks
PCM or relearn issue only after voltage, ground, and command checks pass
quick_checks: Check for limp mode, reduced power message, and related APP/TPS correlation codes
Inspect throttle body bore, plate movement, connector, terminal tension, and harness routing
Graph TPS and APP signals while slowly sweeping the pedal and throttle command
Verify 5V reference, ground, and signal circuits before replacing the throttle body
Clean throttle deposits only when allowed by service information, then perform relearn if required
Confirm repair with stable idle, smooth pedal sweep data, and no reduced-power return
